title: Kyrie Irving ‘close’ to full ACL recovery, weighs in on Knicks making the NBA Finals
content:
Nearly 15 months after he suffered a torn left ACL, Kyrie Irving said he’s almost fully recovered.

“I am definitely close to being over at 100 percent in terms of my ACL recovery,” the Dallas Mavericks point guard said Saturday during a Twitch live stream. “It’s been a while now. It’s been a year and some change. I’m so grateful I’ve had some time to heal and experiment with my body on the court and off the court, in the weight room.”

Irving’s left knee injury caused him to miss the final 20 games of the 2024-25 campaign and all of this season. Irving was in the midst of an All-Star season before he got hurt in March 2025. He averaged 24.7 points on 47.3 percent shooting from the field and 40.1 percent shooting from 3, while also adding 4.8 rebounds and 4.6 assists per game.

Additionally, Irving acknowledged in the live stream that he will be paying attention to the NBA Finals with the New York Knicks returning to the championship round for the first time in 27 years. Irving, who grew up in West Orange, N.J., and spent 3 1/2 seasons with the Brooklyn Nets before being traded to Dallas, praised the play of fellow point guard —and former Maverick — Jalen Brunson and weighed in on the potential atmosphere that the Knicks, in and outside of Madison Square Garden, could provide.

“Knicks fans are gonna go bonkers, man,” Irving said. “Gear up for it if you’re on the East Coast, man. They made it to the NBA Finals. They earned their ticket. … I’m excited to watch them, too.”

Mavericks fans will be more delighted to hear about Irving’s health report, particularly with what the future could hold. Because of his recovery, Irving has yet to suit up alongside Cooper Flagg, the No. 1 pick in the 2025 NBA Draft. Masai Ujiri, the Mavericks new team president, said in May that there is a “huge curiosity” within Dallas’ organization to see Irving, 34, and Flagg, 19, play together, even though there is a 15-year age difference between them.

“Kevin Durant once told me, ‘There is only one Kyrie walking around in the world,’” Ujiri said earlier this month. “I think we have to figure out a way how Kyrie fits with our program. I have had those conversations with Kyrie. I think Kyrie will fit.”

Irving is owed $39.5 million this upcoming season. He holds a $42.4 million player option in the summer of 2027.

The Mavericks are in a tricky spot from a team-building perspective because after this year, they don’t have outright control of their own first-round pick again until 2031. That means they’ll likely have to build around Flagg, their teenage franchise player, by developing the talent already on the roster, trading for players or by acquiring other teams’ picks.

Irving, a former No. 1 pick himself, will enter his 16th year in the league and 15th season playing this fall. The Mavericks are hopeful he can help boost their 27th-ranked offense and be a go-to player in the clutch. Dallas, according to NBA.com, had a 17-28 record last season in “clutch time” — games that were within five points anytime in the last five minutes.

“At this age, I do feel like the game is slowing down,” Irving said. “But I’m also able to do more out there just more efficiently.”
